extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of poetics and dramatic writing; playwrights and creative writers studying classical tragedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama (plot, character, and choral elements) based on Aristotle's Poetics: requirements for unity, magnitude, probability, reversal/recognition, and appropriate emotional effect (pity and fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy as imitation of a complete action of certain magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is 'imitation of an action complete and whole and of a certain magnitude' and must have a beginning, middle, and end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot must form a whole (has an origin, a middle and a termination). The whole need not be large in absolute terms but must have a determinate magnitude (neither too small nor too vast) so that the whole can be apprehended. Example references: Odyssean and Homeric unity; the whole is ruined if a part is removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (single, integral plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fabula/muthos should be essentially one action — the play should imitate one whole action rather than a series of disconnected events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many disparate incidents or multiple unrelated acts destroy the unity and fail to produce a coherent tragedy. If moving or removing a part causes the whole to be confused or collapse, that part is essential — the plot's parts must cohere to produce the single action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate magnitude/length
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy must have 'some magnitude' appropriate to perception and memory: neither trivially short nor excessively long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnitude must be big enough to present a whole action yet concise enough to be grasped in a single view (e.g., contest-time constraints like the clepsydra). The work should preserve a length that is memorable and suitable to the theatre/contest context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and necessity in incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in the plot should arise from necessity or probability (or what is likely), not from mere chance or randomness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions should follow from the antecedent events by necessity or probability so that the sequence is plausible. Poets may invent what could happen (universal), unlike historians who report particulars. Implausible or gratuitous occurrences reduce poetic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of episodic, random inserts (episodic myths)
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodic plots — where episodes follow one another without causal necessity or probability — are judged the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes that are neither probable nor necessary (mere 'incidents' strung together) are characteristic of inferior poets. Good composition requires events to arise from the plot's own constitution rather than being patched in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for complex over simple plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex plots (those involving reversal and/or recognition and a change of fortune) are superior to simple plots (without these features).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complex plot includes peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition), producing wonder and strong emotional effects. Simple plots (continuous without recognition or reversal) are less moving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (reversal) as a dramatic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal is a change to the opposite in the course of the action (a turn of events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peripeteia should arise from the plot's constitution (by necessity or probability) and contribute to the tragic effect; examples include changes in Oedipus' fortunes. Reversal alone can produce marvel if it seems designed rather than merely accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis (recognition) as a dramatic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is the transition from ignorance to knowledge, especially concerning persons' identities or relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The finest recognition is when it accompanies reversal; recognition that follows or coincides with peripeteia produces the strongest pity and fear (e.g., Oedipus recognizing his identity). Recognitions can be of different kinds (between people, regarding objects, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of recognition and reversal to produce pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should arouse pity and fear; a peripeteia accompanied by anagnorisis is especially apt to evoke these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reversal and recognition occur together, the emotional impact is greatest. Such moments are central to tragic imitation and the proper pleasure derived from tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos (suffering) as a necessary element
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathos (suffering, destructive or painful actions such as deaths) is one of the key parts of the plot and contributes to tragic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passion is a change of fortune that produces pain or destruction (deaths, mutilations, etc.). It is one of three parts of the plot along with reversal and recognition. Pathos should be integrated so as to move the audience to pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character change must be appropriate (hamartia, not vice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should not change from good to bad or vice versa in a way that undermines pity and fear; the best is a noble person who falls due to an error (hamartia), not because of vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not tragic to portray the wicked becoming unfortunate or the virtuous becoming wicked; neither inspires pity or fear properly. The ideal tragic figure is one who is 'not eminently good and just, nor through vice and depravity fall into misfortune, but through some error.' This elicits appropriate emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate moral relation of sufferers (friends rather than mere enemies)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most moving actions are those among those who are friends or near to one another (father/son, brother/brother, mother/son), rather than purely hostile relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a wrong is done by an enemy, it lacks pity; if by a friend or kinsman, the same action arouses pity and fear. Use of well-known mythic figures is allowable provided their treatment is artful and not merely derivative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreliance on spectacle (opsis) over plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (visual presentation) is less an art of poetry and more an external contrivance; the poet should not depend primarily on visual effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet's chief tools are plot and character; spectacle and stagecraft are more allied to acting and production. Relying chiefly on spectacle cheapens tragic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry vs history: universality over particularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry states the universal (what could or should happen); history states the particular (what actually happened).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets name and compose likely or necessary actions; historians recount particulars. As such, poets may invent plausible events to exemplify general truths and probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of names and invented elements appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Some names in tragedy may be familiar, some invented; the poet may compose with invented names/elements as art requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiar names can enhance recognition, but poets should not assume that including famous incidents alone makes a good plot; invention and arrangement toward a unified action are what matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization of parts of tragedy (prologue, episode, chorus, exodus, parodos, stasimon, kommos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into parts: prologue (before the chorus enters), episodes (between choral songs), exodus (after which there is no chorus-song), parodos (the chorus' entry-song), stasimon (stationary choral-song), kommos (lamentation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These parts are to be used in composing the work; their order and measure should depend on the quantity and the divisions necessary for the play. The chorus has its medium (song) and its own functions in the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical/choric elements (melody) and their role
rubrics_metrics.description: The choral song (melody) forms part of the tragedy (parodos, stasimon, kommos) and contributes to the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choral music must be integrated and measured appropriately; parodos is the whole first choral song, stasimon is the choral song without pauses or turns, and kommos is a shared lament between chorus and actors. The chorus' contribution should enhance the imitation, not substitute for plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition should imitate terrible and pitiable things (suitable subject-matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best tragic composition imitates things that are terrible and pitiable (resembling misfortune and suffering), as this is proper to the tragic imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material should appear purposeful (as if by design) rather than purely accidental to be more marvelous. Tragedy should not seek every possible pleasure but that which is proper (the pleasure derived from pity and fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking of choices regarding ignorance/knowledge and action
rubrics_metrics.description: There are preferred sequences of ignorance/knowledge and action: e.g., acting in ignorance and then recognition is better than acting knowingly not to act; certain patterns of ignorance, action, and recognition produce stronger effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worst is: a person knows and intends and does not act (leads to ugliness, not the tragic). Better is: one acts in ignorance and recognizes afterward (arouses wonder). The very best examples are nuanced (e.g., where someone intends to kill but does not and then recognizes), so playwrights should arrange the order of ignorance, action, and recognition to maximize marvel and emotional effect (illustrated by Antigone, Iphigenia, Medea episodes).
